title: London System: the pyramid set-up and the plans that grow from it
outcomes: Names the job of each piece in the London set-up (triangle of pawns on c3, d4 and e3, bishop outside the chain, knights behind it, bishop on d3) and says which pawn recaptures on g3
Applies three conditions before the pawn break on e4 (guards against attackers, developed pieces, lines that open for White) and sees why it fails with the knight still on b1
Chooses between the e4 break and the knight jump to e5 for the position in front of them, with the d4 pawn as the support for the jump
Avoids h4 when the h-pawn is needed to recapture on g3, and says what the f-pawn recapture costs
Answers Black's c-pawn advance against the bishop on d3 by retreating along the same diagonal
Quotes our own counts for the plans with their sample sizes, and says what the counts do and do not show

steps.caption: White to move after eight moves each. Every minor piece is developed, White has not castled yet and the pawns in the centre are guarded. Count the pieces that watch e4 for each side, then think about what a pawn move there would do. Which plan would you try?

claims.statement: Two white pieces attack e4: the bishop on d3 and the knight on d2.
Two black units attack e4: the pawn on d5 and the knight on f6.
White's dark-squared bishop stands on g3, outside the pawn chain.

steps.prompt: Before any explanation: write the plan you would try for White here, and what you think Black wants to do. You will come back to this at the end.

steps.text: **The question of this lesson.** Why does White build the same set-up against almost any Black reply, and what does it let White do next? [I] A fixed set-up saves thinking in the first eight moves. By the end you can say what each piece guards, choose between the pawn break on e4, the knight jump to e5 and the trade on g3, and avoid h4 while Black's bishop can trade on g3.

steps.caption: The set-up starts with the bishop. Step through the first three moves, and see why the bishop comes out before the pawn goes to e3.

line.say: The pawn takes space and opens the diagonal of the c1 bishop.
Black answers in kind.
The bishop comes out first, outside the pawns. Once the pawn is on e3 it could reach only d2.

claims.statement: After three moves the bishop stands on f4, outside the pawn chain.
If the pawn went to e3 first, the bishop on c1 would have just one legal move, to d2.

steps.caption: Black to move. Now the pawn on e3 is safe to play, because the bishop is already outside it.

line.say: Black develops the knight.
The pawn supports d4 and opens the way for the king's bishop.
Black opens the diagonal of the f8 bishop.

claims.statement: After the three moves a white pawn stands on e3.

steps.caption: Step through the set-up from the position after 4.Nf3 Bd6 (both knights out). Each white move has one job: guard d4, add a guard of e4, or keep the bishop outside.

line.say: The bishop leaves f4 before it can be traded, and still aims along the diagonal toward d6.
Black castles.
The queen's knight develops behind the pawns and will help to fight for e4.

steps.caption: Black to move. Black attacks d4 twice; watch how White completes the triangle.

line.say: Black attacks the pawn on d4 from the side.
The c-pawn guards d4 and completes the triangle with the e3 pawn.
Black adds a second attacker on d4.

claims.statement: After these moves, the pawns on c3, d4 and e3 are all protected by another pawn.

steps.caption: White to move. The last two moves of the set-up add a guard of e4 and prepare the long diagonal.

line.say: The bishop adds a second piece against e4 and looks toward h7.
Black prepares to place a bishop on the long diagonal.

claims.statement: At the end the bishop on d3 and the knight on d2 attack e4 together.
At depth 16 White stands slightly better, by a fraction of a pawn.

steps.text: **The shape.** White's pawns on c3, d4 and e3 form a triangle: c3 and e3 guard d4, and f2 guards e3. The bishop on g3 stands outside it, the knights on f3 and d2 stand behind it, and the bishop on d3 looks toward the kingside. [I] Nothing in the centre needs defending, so every piece is free to prepare one pawn break.

steps.caption: Black may offer a trade on g3. Step through it and watch which pawn recaptures.

line.say: Black offers the bishop trade. The bishop on g3 is attacked, and it is guarded by two pawns, f2 and h2.
The h-pawn recaptures. The structure stays whole, the g-pawn moves to g3 and a rook can use the h-file.

claims.statement: After the trade and the recapture, the h-file is half-open for White: White has no h-pawn and Black still has one.
At depth 16 the position after the trade is close to level.

steps.caption: White does not have to wait. Step through the trade on d6 and see what changes for the dark-squared bishop.

line.say: White can also trade first on d6, removing the bishop that attacks the other bishop.
The queen recaptures and now looks along the diagonal toward g3 and h2.

claims.statement: At depth 16 the position after White trades first is close to level.
After the trade neither side has the bishop pair.

steps.text: **Keep the bishop or let it be traded?** [I] The bishop on g3 is safe because the h-pawn can recapture, so Black's trade costs White nothing structurally and opens the h-file. White can also keep the bishop. Black can choose: in our online data (3,375 games reaching 5.Bg3) Black castled in 1,214 and traded in 693. [H] The h-file is useful only when Black's king is on that side; the data cannot test that.

**Plan 1: the pawn break on e4.** [I] Three conditions. One: count the guards of e4. White has the knight on d2 and the bishop on d3; Black has the pawn on d5 and the knight on f6. Two: the pieces behind the pawn are developed, so nothing hangs. Three: the exchanges open lines for White's pieces. If one condition fails, the push costs material or leaves White worse.
steps.chapter: Plan 1: the pawn break on e4

steps.caption: The break in action. Step through the first exchange and count the attackers of e4 at each move.

line.say: The pawn steps up. It is attacked twice and guarded twice, once by the knight and once by the bishop.
Black takes the pawn, and now the knight and the bishop both attack the pawn on e4.
The knight recaptures. The exchanges so far are even.

claims.statement: Before the push, two white pieces attack e4: the bishop on d3 and the knight on d2.
Two black units also attack e4: the pawn on d5 and the knight on f6.

steps.caption: Black to move. Step through the second exchange and see where the bishop ends up.

line.say: Black trades knights.
The bishop recaptures and is now strongly placed, aimed at the black kingside. White has opened the centre on its own terms.

claims.statement: At depth 16 White stands better by a fraction of a pawn after the exchanges.
At the end a white bishop stands on e4.

steps.caption: Black does not have to capture. Step through the quiet reply and see what the pawn on e5 gains.

line.say: Black declines. A pawn on e5 would attack both the bishop and the knight, so the bishop steps back first.
The pawn advances and attacks the knight, which loses its best square.

steps.caption: Black to move. The knight is attacked: step through the retreat and the jump.

line.say: The knight goes to the rim, where it attacks the bishop on g3.
The knight jumps to g5 and, with the bishop on d3, aims at the pawn on h7.

claims.statement: At depth 16 White stands slightly better after the knight jump.
At the end two white pieces attack the pawn on h7.

steps.title: Is the break on e4 sound?
steps.prompt: Predict first. The first position is the one you started with. In the second only the queen's knight has moved: it is back on b1. Decide for each whether the pawn push works, and name the condition that decides it. Not sure? Use the hints for an example first.

steps.text: **What our games say.** [V] After the bishop reaches d3, our masters data (329,379 games, both players 2500 or more) shows Black playing b6 in 123 games, queen to e7 in 35 and g6 in 15. After b6, White played queen to e2 in 63, e4 in 32, knight to e5 in 20 and castled in 8. [I] More than one plan is playable; the counts are choices, not proof, and each plan has only a few dozen games.

steps.caption: The same break with one more guard. Step through the queen move, the bishop move and the push, and count the guards of e4.

line.say: The most common choice in our masters data. The queen will be a third guard of e4 as soon as the pawn moves.
Black develops the bishop onto the long diagonal.
Now the pawn is guarded three times and attacked only twice, since the knight on c6 blocks the new bishop.

claims.statement: After the queen move, two pieces attack e4 (the bishop and the knight); the queen on e2 backs up e4 only once the pawn has moved there.
Black attacks e4 twice: the bishop on b7 is blocked by its own knight on c6.

steps.caption: Black to move. Step through the exchanges; the queen will take back on e4.

line.say: Black takes.
The knight recaptures.
Black trades knights. The queen takes back on e4 next, so the exchanges end level.

claims.statement: At depth 16 White stands slightly better after the queen move and the exchanges.

steps.caption: The knight jump. Here Black has put the queen on e7 instead of playing b6. Step through the first three moves of the fight over e5.

line.say: The knight jumps to the square the d4 pawn guards. It attacks the knight on c6 and the pawn on f7.
Black offers a trade to remove the intruder.
The other knight returns to f3, so e5 stays covered and White can choose when to trade.

claims.statement: After the jump the knight on e5 attacks c6, d7 and f7.
The pawn on d4 guards the square e5.

steps.chapter: Plan 2: the knight jump to e5

steps.caption: Black to move. Step through the pawn move and the trade that follows.

line.say: Black takes the e4 square with a pawn, which loosens the pawn on e6.
The knight takes on c6 and forces a recapture that changes Black's structure.
Black recaptures with the b-pawn. Black now has doubled pawns on the c-file.

claims.statement: At depth 16 White stands slightly better at the end of the line.
At the end Black has doubled pawns on the c-file.

steps.text: **Choosing a plan.** [I] The e4 break needs the knight and the bishop behind it, and it opens the centre. The knight jump needs the d4 pawn behind it, and it keeps the centre closed. [H] I suspect the break suits positions where Black has put the c8 bishop behind a b6 pawn, and the jump suits positions where the black queen stands on the e-file; the counts above fit that guess but cannot test it.

steps.prompt: Do you agree with the [H]? Which of the two plans would you choose against a player who keeps the queen at home, and why?

steps.caption: A pawn move to avoid while the black bishop eyes g3. Step through what h4 allows and ask which pawn recaptures after the trade.

line.say: The pawn advances to prepare h5, but it leaves h2, the square from which it recaptures on g3. The problem is the bishop on d6, not the move itself.
Black trades. The h-pawn can no longer take back.
The f-pawn must recapture, which doubles the g-pawns and leaves e3 without its guard.

claims.statement: The move is at least 1.6 pawns worse than the best move at depth 16.
After the f-pawn recaptures, the white pawns on g2 and g3 are doubled.

steps.caption: Black to move. Step through the attack on the weak pawn on g3.

line.say: The queen aims at the weak pawn on g3.
White castles and cannot hold everything.
Black takes the pawn. White has lost a pawn for nothing.

claims.statement: At depth 16 Black stands better by about two pawns at the end of the line.

steps.caption: The other side of the board. Black's counter is to grab space with the c-pawn. Step through it and see what White keeps.

line.say: Black's idea: attack the bishop and gain space on the queenside.
The bishop retreats and keeps its diagonal toward the kingside.
Black gains more space on the queenside. White keeps the pawn chain solid, and the break on e4 is still available.

claims.statement: After the pawn move, a black pawn on c4 attacks the bishop on d3.
At depth 16 White stands slightly better after the bishop retreat and the queenside space gain.

steps.text: **Before you choose.** Ask three things. Is the pawn I want to move the one that recaptures later? How many pieces guard the square a break will use, and how many attack it? Which of Black's moves just made one plan better than another? The test mixes the plans, and one position is a mistake.

**What to remember.**
- White builds a triangle of pawns, c3, d4 and e3, and puts the bishop outside it.
- The h-pawn recaptures on g3, so keep it at home.
- The e4 break needs two guards, developed pieces and open lines for you.
- The knight jump to e5 needs the d4 pawn behind it.
- Count guards, check which pawn recaptures, then choose a plan.

steps.prompt: Teach it back. Imagine you teach a friend who knows how the pieces move. Write five sentences: (1) what the triangle of pawns does, (2) the three conditions for the e4 break, (3) why the h-pawn must stay on h2, (4) when the knight jump is better, (5) one warning to give.

steps.text: **Self-check.** Did you give conditions, not just moves? Did you say what fails when a condition is missing? Did you give a position a friend could set up on a board? Did you name the pawn that recaptures? The app grades nothing: compare your five sentences with these four questions and fix the weakest one.

steps.prompt: Go back to your first answer in the hook. Rewrite it in a better sentence: your plan, and the condition it needs.
